questiontext.text: Integration testing primarily aims to expose faults in:

answer.text: The interactions and interfaces between modules that are combined together

feedback.text: Correct — integration testing targets the way separately-developed modules work together.

answer.text: The internal logic of a single isolated function

feedback.text: That is unit testing; integration testing assumes units already work and focuses on their interactions.

answer.text: The behaviour of the complete system against user requirements

feedback.text: That is system testing, which comes after integration.

answer.text: The response time of the program under heavy load

feedback.text: That is performance/load testing, a non-functional concern, not integration.

generalfeedback.text: Integration testing verifies that modules which have already passed unit testing cooperate correctly once combined — it hunts for interface and interaction faults, not for logic bugs inside a single unit.

questiontext.text: In the usual ordering of test levels, integration testing sits:

answer.text: After unit testing and before system testing

feedback.text: Correct — units are tested first, then integrated and tested together, then the whole system.

answer.text: Before unit testing

feedback.text: Units must pass unit testing first, otherwise interaction failures cannot be distinguished from unit bugs.

answer.text: After system testing

feedback.text: System testing is the last of these three levels, not before integration.

answer.text: It replaces unit testing entirely

feedback.text: Integration testing complements unit testing; it does not replace it.

generalfeedback.text: The common progression is unit → integration → system. Integration testing builds on already unit-tested modules and precedes end-to-end system testing.

questiontext.text: Big-bang integration means:

answer.text: All modules are combined at once and the whole assembly is tested together

feedback.text: Correct — big-bang integrates everything in a single step.

answer.text: Modules are added one at a time from the top of the hierarchy downward

feedback.text: That is top-down incremental integration, not big-bang.

answer.text: Modules are added one at a time from the leaves upward

feedback.text: That is bottom-up incremental integration, not big-bang.

answer.text: Each module is tested completely in isolation before any are combined

feedback.text: That describes unit testing; big-bang is about combining all units simultaneously.

generalfeedback.text: Big-bang (non-incremental) integration assembles all modules together and tests them as one. It needs little scaffolding but makes failures hard to localise.

questiontext.text: Top-down integration proceeds by:

answer.text: Integrating from the top of the call hierarchy downward, using stubs for not-yet-integrated lower modules

feedback.text: Correct — the top control modules come first; their callees are stubbed until integrated.

answer.text: Integrating from the leaf modules upward, using drivers

feedback.text: That is bottom-up integration.

answer.text: Combining all modules at once

feedback.text: That is big-bang integration.

answer.text: Testing each module in isolation with no other modules present

feedback.text: That is unit testing, not an integration strategy.

generalfeedback.text: Top-down integration starts at the top (main control) module and works down the hierarchy. Lower modules that are not yet integrated are represented by stubs.

questiontext.text: Bottom-up integration proceeds by:

answer.text: Integrating from the leaf modules upward, using drivers to call the modules under test

feedback.text: Correct — low-level modules are integrated first, driven by temporary drivers.

answer.text: Integrating from the top control module downward, using stubs

feedback.text: That is top-down integration.

answer.text: Combining all modules simultaneously

feedback.text: That is big-bang integration.

answer.text: Delivering the software to end users to find faults

feedback.text: That is closer to acceptance/field testing, not bottom-up integration.

generalfeedback.text: Bottom-up integration starts with the lowest-level (leaf) modules and works up the hierarchy. Because their callers are not yet present, a driver is written to invoke each module under test.

questiontext.text: Sandwich (hybrid) integration is best described as:

answer.text: Combining top-down and bottom-up, working from both ends toward the middle at the same time

feedback.text: Correct — the top layers use stubs while the bottom layers use drivers, meeting in the middle.

answer.text: Combining all modules at once with no stubs or drivers

feedback.text: That is big-bang integration.

answer.text: Strictly top-down with no bottom-up element

feedback.text: Pure top-down is not hybrid; sandwich mixes both directions.

answer.text: Testing only the middle layer and ignoring the top and bottom

feedback.text: Sandwich integrates all layers; it does not ignore the ends.

generalfeedback.text: Sandwich (hybrid) integration applies top-down to the upper layers (with stubs) and bottom-up to the lower layers (with drivers) simultaneously, converging on a target middle layer.

questiontext.text: A stub in integration testing is a temporary piece of code that:

answer.text: Stands in for a lower-level module that the module under test calls

feedback.text: Correct — a stub is called by the module under test and returns canned results.

answer.text: Stands in for a higher-level module that calls the module under test

feedback.text: That is a driver, not a stub.

answer.text: Is the final production version of a called module

feedback.text: A stub is a throwaway substitute, not the real module.

answer.text: Is a defect deliberately injected into the code

feedback.text: That describes a mutant/seeded fault, not a stub.

generalfeedback.text: A stub replaces a not-yet-integrated callee: the module under test calls it, and it returns simplified, pre-arranged values. Stubs are what top-down integration needs.

questiontext.text: A driver in integration testing is a temporary piece of code that:

answer.text: Stands in for a higher-level module and calls the module under test

feedback.text: Correct — a driver is the caller: it invokes the module under test and passes inputs.

answer.text: Stands in for a lower-level module that the module under test calls

feedback.text: That is a stub, not a driver.

answer.text: Is the production main program shipped to users

feedback.text: A driver is a throwaway harness, not the real caller.

answer.text: Is a tool that measures code coverage

feedback.text: That is a coverage tool, unrelated to a driver's role.

generalfeedback.text: A driver replaces a not-yet-integrated caller: it calls the module under test, supplies inputs, and checks outputs. Drivers are what bottom-up integration needs.

questiontext.text: An interface (integration) fault is a defect that:

answer.text: Arises from an incorrect assumption or mismatch in how two modules communicate

feedback.text: Correct — e.g. wrong parameter type/order, a violated protocol, or inconsistent shared state.

answer.text: Is a purely internal logic error confined to one module

feedback.text: That is a unit-level fault; interface faults are about communication between modules.

answer.text: Is a spelling mistake in the user documentation

feedback.text: Documentation typos are not interface faults between software modules.

answer.text: Is a hardware failure in the CPU

feedback.text: That is a hardware fault, not a software interface fault.

generalfeedback.text: Interface faults surface when integrated modules interact: mismatched parameter lists, wrong call order, protocol/timing violations, or inconsistent assumptions about shared data. These are exactly what integration testing hunts for.

questiontext.text: Which integration strategy characteristically requires stubs?

answer.text: Top-down

feedback.text: Correct — top-down integrates upper modules first, so their not-yet-integrated callees are stubbed.

answer.text: Bottom-up

feedback.text: Bottom-up needs drivers, not stubs, because it starts from the leaves.

answer.text: Big-bang

feedback.text: Big-bang assembles everything at once and typically avoids per-step stubs.

answer.text: None of these ever uses stubs

feedback.text: Top-down relies on stubs, so this is wrong.

generalfeedback.text: Top-down integrates from the top down; the lower modules a top module calls are not ready yet, so they are replaced by stubs. (Bottom-up pairs with drivers.)

questiontext.text: Which integration strategy characteristically requires drivers?

answer.text: Bottom-up

feedback.text: Correct — bottom-up integrates leaf modules first, so a driver is written to call each one.

answer.text: Top-down

feedback.text: Top-down needs stubs, not drivers, because it starts from the top control module.

answer.text: Big-bang

feedback.text: Big-bang combines all modules at once and typically avoids per-step drivers.

answer.text: None of these ever uses drivers

feedback.text: Bottom-up relies on drivers, so this is wrong.

generalfeedback.text: Bottom-up integrates from the leaves up; the higher modules that would call them are not ready yet, so a driver is written to invoke each module under test. (Top-down pairs with stubs.)

name.text: A stub is called by the module under test

questiontext.text: A stub is called by the module under test (the module under test invokes the stub).

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — a stub is a substitute callee, so the module under test calls it.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: A stub does sit below the module under test and is called by it; the caller-side substitute is the driver.

generalfeedback.text: Direction matters: a stub is below and is called by the module under test (a substitute callee); a driver is above and calls the module under test (a substitute caller).

name.text: A driver is called by the module under test

questiontext.text: A driver is called by the module under test (the module under test invokes the driver).

answer.text: true

feedback.text: This reverses the direction — a driver calls the module under test, not the other way round.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — a driver is the caller: it calls the module under test. The thing the module under test calls is a stub.

generalfeedback.text: A driver stands in for a higher-level caller, so it calls the module under test. Only a stub is called by the module under test.

questiontext.text: During integration, a stub substitutes for:

answer.text: A not-yet-integrated lower-level module that the module under test calls

feedback.text: Correct — the stub takes the place of an absent callee.

answer.text: A not-yet-integrated higher-level module that calls the module under test

feedback.text: That absent caller is replaced by a driver, not a stub.

answer.text: A test oracle that decides pass or fail

feedback.text: An oracle judges results; it is not a stand-in for a module.

answer.text: The database used by the whole system

feedback.text: A stub is a code substitute for a called module, not a data store in general.

generalfeedback.text: A stub replaces a missing callee — a lower module the module under test would call. Top-down integration relies on stubs while the lower levels are still absent.

questiontext.text: During integration, a driver substitutes for:

answer.text: A not-yet-integrated higher-level module that calls the module under test

feedback.text: Correct — the driver takes the place of an absent caller.

answer.text: A not-yet-integrated lower-level module that the module under test calls

feedback.text: That absent callee is replaced by a stub, not a driver.

answer.text: A compiler that builds the modules

feedback.text: A driver is a test harness, not a build tool.

answer.text: A defect report filed by a user

feedback.text: That is unrelated to what a driver stands in for.

generalfeedback.text: A driver replaces a missing caller — a higher module that would invoke the module under test. Bottom-up integration relies on drivers while the upper levels are still absent.

questiontext.text: Consider this call tree: A calls B and C (A is the root; B and C are its only children). Using top-down integration, step 1 integrates the root A and stubs its not-yet-integrated direct children. How many stubs are needed at step 1?

feedback.text: Correct — A directly calls B and C, so both are stubbed: 2 stubs.
A has two direct children (B and C), so one stub is not enough.
Only B and C are directly called by A; there is no third child.
Top-down step 1 must stub A's callees, and A calls two modules.

generalfeedback.text: Top-down step 1 integrates the root A alone; every module A directly calls must be stubbed. A calls B and C, so 2 stubs are needed.

questiontext.text: Consider this call tree: M calls N, O, and P (M is the root with three children). Using top-down integration, how many stubs are needed at step 1 (integrating M alone)?

feedback.text: Correct — M directly calls N, O, and P, so all three are stubbed: 3 stubs.
M has three direct children, not one.
There are three direct children (N, O, P), so two stubs is too few.
M calls exactly three modules; there is no fourth.

generalfeedback.text: Top-down step 1 integrates M and stubs each module it directly calls. M calls N, O, and P, so 3 stubs are needed.

name.text: Bottom-up driver for a single leaf

questiontext.text: Consider this call tree: A calls B and C; B calls D (so D is a leaf). Using bottom-up integration, you integrate the leaf D first. How many drivers are needed to integrate D?

feedback.text: Correct — D's real caller (B) is not integrated yet, so one driver is written to call D.
Something must call D; since B is not ready, a driver is required.
Only one module (D) is under test, so one driver suffices.

answer.text: 1 stub

feedback.text: Bottom-up uses drivers, not stubs; and D has no callees to stub.

generalfeedback.text: Bottom-up integrates leaves first. D has no callees (no stubs needed), but its caller B is absent, so one driver is written to invoke D: 1 driver.

name.text: Top-down stubs when integrating an intermediate module

questiontext.text: Consider this call tree: R calls X and Y; X calls Z. Using top-down integration you have already integrated R, and now you integrate X. How many stubs must be in place for X's own not-yet-integrated callees?

feedback.text: Correct — X directly calls only Z, which is not yet integrated, so one stub (for Z) is needed.
Y is a sibling of X, not a callee of X; X calls only Z.
X calls Z, and Z is not integrated yet, so a stub for Z is required.
X has a single callee (Z); there are not three.

generalfeedback.text: When integrating X top-down, only X's direct callees that are still absent must be stubbed. X calls only Z, so 1 stub is needed. (Y is R's other child, unrelated to X's callees.)

questiontext.text: Consider this call tree: A calls B and C, where B and C are both leaves. Using bottom-up integration with one driver per module under test, how many drivers are needed to integrate B and C as the first step?

feedback.text: Correct — one driver per module under test, and two leaf modules (B and C) are being integrated: 2 drivers.
Two separate modules are under test; with one driver per module that is two drivers.
Their caller A is not integrated yet, so drivers are required to invoke B and C.

answer.text: 2 stubs

feedback.text: Bottom-up uses drivers, not stubs; and leaves B and C have no callees to stub.

generalfeedback.text: Bottom-up integrates leaves first. B and C are leaves whose caller A is absent, so with one driver per module under test, 2 drivers are needed.

questiontext.text: Compared with big-bang, incremental integration generally gives:

answer.text: Better fault isolation, because a failure points to the newly added module or its interface

feedback.text: Correct — adding modules one at a time localises where a new failure came from.

answer.text: Worse fault isolation, because more scaffolding is used

feedback.text: Extra stubs/drivers do not worsen isolation; incremental integration improves it.

answer.text: No difference in fault isolation

feedback.text: There is a clear difference: incremental isolates faults far better than big-bang.

answer.text: Guaranteed absence of interface faults

feedback.text: No strategy guarantees the absence of faults; it only makes them easier to locate.

generalfeedback.text: Because incremental integration adds one module at a time, a new failure is most likely due to the module just added or its interface — so faults are much easier to isolate than in big-bang, where everything is combined at once.

name.text: Which strategy tests top-level control earliest

questiontext.text: Which strategy exercises the top-level control logic earliest?

answer.text: Top-down

feedback.text: Correct — top-down integrates the main control module first, so control logic is tested early.

answer.text: Bottom-up

feedback.text: Bottom-up tests leaves first; the top-level control logic is integrated last.

answer.text: Big-bang

feedback.text: Big-bang tests everything only after all modules are combined, not the top earliest.

answer.text: None can test control logic early

feedback.text: Top-down does exactly this by integrating the top module first.

generalfeedback.text: Top-down starts at the main control module, so high-level control flow and major design decisions are exercised early — one of its main advantages.

name.text: Which strategy tests leaf utilities earliest

questiontext.text: Which strategy exercises the low-level leaf/utility modules earliest?

answer.text: Bottom-up

feedback.text: Correct — bottom-up integrates leaf modules first, so utilities are tested early.

answer.text: Top-down

feedback.text: Top-down tests the top first; leaf utilities are integrated (or only stubbed) until late.

answer.text: Big-bang

feedback.text: Big-bang exercises everything only after all modules are combined.

answer.text: None can test leaves early

feedback.text: Bottom-up does exactly this by integrating the leaves first.

generalfeedback.text: Bottom-up starts at the leaves, so low-level utility modules are thoroughly exercised early — useful when those utilities are complex or critical.

questiontext.text: A team integrates all modules at once (big-bang) and a test fails. Why is diagnosing the failure typically hard?

answer.text: Any of the many simultaneously-combined interfaces could be the cause, so the fault is hard to localise

feedback.text: Correct — with everything combined at once, poor fault isolation makes the cause hard to pin down.

answer.text: Big-bang produces no test output to examine

feedback.text: It still produces output; the problem is isolating which interface failed, not a lack of output.

answer.text: Stubs and drivers hide the real modules

feedback.text: Big-bang uses little scaffolding; the difficulty is the many interfaces combined at once.

answer.text: Big-bang cannot detect interface faults at all

feedback.text: It can detect them; it just makes them hard to locate.

generalfeedback.text: Big-bang combines all modules together, so when a failure appears any of the numerous interfaces could be responsible. This poor fault isolation is big-bang's main drawback.

questiontext.text: A frequently cited advantage of top-down integration is that:

answer.text: An early working skeleton of the system is available, since the top control structure is built first

feedback.text: Correct — a partial, demonstrable program emerges early.

answer.text: No stubs are ever required

feedback.text: Top-down actually depends on stubs for its lower modules.

answer.text: Low-level utility modules are fully tested first

feedback.text: That is a bottom-up characteristic, not top-down.

answer.text: It removes the need for any regression testing

feedback.text: Regression testing is still needed as modules are added.

generalfeedback.text: Because top-down builds the upper control structure first, an early demonstrable skeleton of the program appears, letting stakeholders see progress and letting major design errors surface early.

questiontext.text: A drawback of bottom-up integration is that:

answer.text: The top-level control logic and user interface are integrated and tested last

feedback.text: Correct — high-level control and UI concerns surface late, so major design errors there appear late.

answer.text: It cannot test leaf modules

feedback.text: Bottom-up tests leaf modules first; that is its strength, not a weakness.

answer.text: It requires stubs for every leaf

feedback.text: Bottom-up uses drivers, not stubs, and leaves have no callees to stub.

answer.text: It combines all modules at once

feedback.text: That describes big-bang, not bottom-up.

generalfeedback.text: Since bottom-up integrates leaves first and the top last, the main control logic and user interface are exercised only late, so serious high-level design faults may be discovered late.

questiontext.text: Consider this call tree: A calls B, C, and D (B, C, D are all leaves). Using bottom-up integration, how many drivers are needed to integrate just leaf B?

feedback.text: Correct — only B is under test, and its caller A is absent, so one driver is needed.
Only B is being integrated here, not C and D, so one driver suffices.
A is not integrated yet, so something must call B — a driver is required.
A single module under test needs a single driver.

generalfeedback.text: Integrating only leaf B: B has no callees (no stubs), and its caller A is absent, so exactly 1 driver is required to invoke B.

name.text: Top-down step 1 stubs with a grandchild

questiontext.text: Consider this call tree: S calls T and U; T calls V. Using top-down integration, how many stubs are needed at step 1 (integrating the root S alone)?

feedback.text: Correct — at step 1 only S's direct children (T and U) are stubbed; V is not directly called by S.
V is a callee of T, not of S; at step 1 only S's direct children are stubbed.
S has two direct children (T and U), so one stub is not enough.
Step 1 must stub S's direct callees, and S calls two modules.

generalfeedback.text: Top-down step 1 integrates S and stubs only the modules S directly calls: T and U (2 stubs). V is reached only through T, which is not yet integrated, so V is not stubbed at step 1.

questiontext.text: In general, big-bang integration requires fewer temporary stubs and drivers than incremental integration.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — big-bang combines all real modules at once, so it needs little per-step scaffolding; the trade-off is much poorer fault isolation.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Big-bang does typically need less scaffolding; it just pays for it with poor fault isolation.

generalfeedback.text: Because big-bang assembles all the real modules together, it avoids most of the per-step stubs and drivers that incremental integration needs. Its cost is elsewhere: when something fails, isolating the responsible interface is hard.

name.text: Top-down stubs for two children of a subtree

questiontext.text: Consider this call tree: A calls B and C; C calls D and E. Using top-down integration, A and B are already integrated and you now integrate C. How many stubs must be in place for C's own not-yet-integrated callees?

feedback.text: Correct — C directly calls D and E, neither of which is integrated yet, so 2 stubs.
C has two direct callees (D and E), so one stub is too few.
C calls only D and E; B is A's other child, not a callee of C.
C's callees D and E are absent, so stubs are required for them.

generalfeedback.text: When integrating C top-down, only C's direct callees still absent must be stubbed. C calls D and E, so 2 stubs are needed.

name.text: Top-down stubs at a multi-level step

questiontext.text: Consider this call tree: A calls B and C; B calls D and E; C calls F. Using top-down integration, suppose the integrated set is exactly {A, B}. How many stubs must be in place at this point?

feedback.text: Correct — integrated modules call three absent modules: A calls C (stub), and B calls D and E (two stubs) → 3 stubs.
Do not forget A still calls C: stubs are needed for C, D, and E — three in total.
F is called by C, which is not integrated, so F is not stubbed yet; the count is 3.
Both A and B have absent callees; there are three such callees (C, D, E).

generalfeedback.text: With integrated set {A, B}, list every call from an integrated module to a non-integrated one: A→C, B→D, B→E. (A→B is real.) That is stubs for C, D, and E = 3 stubs. F is not stubbed because its caller C is not integrated.

questiontext.text: Consider this call tree: A calls B and C; B calls D and E; C calls F. Using bottom-up integration with one driver per module under test, how many drivers are needed to integrate all the leaf modules as the first step?

feedback.text: Correct — the leaves are D, E, and F; with one driver each that is 3 drivers.
There are three leaves (D, E, F), not two.
Only the leaf modules are integrated at the first step; B and C are not leaves.
Bottom-up uses one driver per leaf under test; there are three leaves, so 3 drivers.

generalfeedback.text: The leaves (modules that call nothing) are D, E, and F. Bottom-up integrates the leaves first, one driver per module under test, so 3 drivers are needed.

questiontext.text: Why might a team choose sandwich (hybrid) integration over pure top-down or pure bottom-up?

answer.text: It lets high-level and low-level modules be integrated in parallel, combining top-down's early control testing with bottom-up's early utility testing

feedback.text: Correct — working from both ends at once gains the benefits of both directions and can shorten the schedule.

answer.text: It eliminates the need for both stubs and drivers

feedback.text: Sandwich uses stubs (upper layers) and drivers (lower layers) — it needs both.

answer.text: It integrates all modules at once like big-bang

feedback.text: Sandwich is incremental from both ends, not a single big-bang step.

answer.text: It guarantees no interface faults will remain

feedback.text: No strategy guarantees the absence of faults.

generalfeedback.text: Sandwich applies top-down to the upper layers (stubs) and bottom-up to the lower layers (drivers) simultaneously, so control logic and utility modules are both exercised early and the two efforts can proceed in parallel.

questiontext.text: A recognised weakness of sandwich integration is that:

answer.text: The middle-layer modules where the two ends meet may get less thorough isolated testing

feedback.text: Correct — because both ends converge on the middle, that target layer can be under-tested in isolation.

answer.text: It cannot test the top-level control logic

feedback.text: Its top-down half exercises the control logic early; that is a strength.

answer.text: It needs neither stubs nor drivers

feedback.text: Sandwich needs both stubs and drivers, so this is false.

answer.text: It provides worse fault isolation than big-bang

feedback.text: Being incremental, sandwich isolates faults better than big-bang, not worse.

generalfeedback.text: Because top-down and bottom-up converge on a middle target layer, those middle modules can end up tested mostly as part of larger assemblies rather than thoroughly in isolation — the main criticism of the sandwich approach.

name.text: Why top-down can hide low-level defects

questiontext.text: Why can top-down integration hide defects that live in low-level modules?

answer.text: Stubs return simplified canned results, so the real low-level behaviour (and its bugs) is not exercised until the stub is replaced

feedback.text: Correct — an oversimplified stub can mask a defect that only the real module would reveal.

answer.text: Top-down never executes the low-level modules at all

feedback.text: They are eventually integrated; the issue is that stubs stand in for them for a long time.

answer.text: Drivers suppress the outputs of low-level modules

feedback.text: Top-down uses stubs, not drivers, and stubs — not drivers — cause the masking here.

answer.text: Low-level defects are always equivalent and undetectable

feedback.text: They are ordinary defects; they are simply not exercised while a stub substitutes for the real module.

generalfeedback.text: Because top-down replaces lower modules with stubs that return canned values, the real (possibly buggy) low-level logic is not run until late. An oversimplified stub can therefore mask a defect that only surfaces once the actual module is integrated.

questiontext.text: In bottom-up integration, why might a serious flaw in the user interface or overall control flow be discovered late?

answer.text: The top-level control and UI modules are integrated last, so faults in them surface only near the end

feedback.text: Correct — bottom-up leaves the top for last, delaying discovery of high-level design faults.

answer.text: Drivers permanently replace the UI modules

feedback.text: Drivers are temporary; the point is that the real UI/control modules are integrated only late.

answer.text: Bottom-up never tests the top-level modules

feedback.text: It does test them — just last, after the lower levels.

answer.text: UI faults are always interface faults, which bottom-up ignores

feedback.text: Bottom-up does test interfaces; the delay is due to integration order, not ignoring faults.

generalfeedback.text: Bottom-up integrates leaves first and the top control/UI modules last, so major high-level design or interface flaws in those top modules are not exercised until late in the integration schedule.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is an example of an interface (integration) fault?

answer.text: Module A calls B as B(width, height) but B expects B(height, width), so the arguments are swapped

feedback.text: Correct — mismatched parameter order across a call boundary is a classic interface fault.

answer.text: A loop inside module B iterates one time too few (an off-by-one within B)

feedback.text: That is an internal logic (unit) fault confined to B, not an interface fault.

answer.text: A local variable inside A is left uninitialised and never passed out

feedback.text: That is an internal fault in A; it does not concern the A–B interface.

answer.text: B computes the wrong result even when called with correct arguments

feedback.text: That is a logic fault inside B, a unit-level concern, not an interface mismatch.

generalfeedback.text: Interface faults occur at the boundary between modules. Passing arguments in the wrong order (a parameter mismatch) is a textbook example — the modules disagree on how they communicate.

questiontext.text: Module A sends data to module B before B has finished initialising, so B occasionally processes garbage. This is best classified as:

answer.text: An interface fault of the timing/protocol kind

feedback.text: Correct — the modules violate the expected order/timing of their interaction.

answer.text: An internal logic fault inside B's computation

feedback.text: B's computation may be fine; the fault is in when A interacts with B — a timing/protocol issue at the interface.

answer.text: A compiler optimisation error

feedback.text: This is about module interaction order, not the compiler.

answer.text: An equivalent mutant

feedback.text: That is a mutation-testing concept, unrelated to an integration timing fault.

generalfeedback.text: When modules disagree on the order or timing of their exchanges — sending before the peer is ready — the defect lies at the interface: a protocol/timing interface fault, exactly what integration testing targets.

questiontext.text: Modules A and B both read and write a shared global counter, each assuming it alone modifies it, and they corrupt each other's value. This is best classified as:

answer.text: An interface fault arising from inconsistent assumptions about shared state

feedback.text: Correct — the modules interact through shared data with conflicting assumptions, an interface fault.

answer.text: A pure unit fault inside A only

feedback.text: The problem emerges from A and B interacting via shared data, not from A alone.

answer.text: A performance fault

feedback.text: The issue is incorrect results from shared-state conflict, not speed.

answer.text: A documentation fault

feedback.text: The defect is in the code's shared-state interaction, not in the docs.

generalfeedback.text: Shared-state (shared-data) faults happen when integrated modules make inconsistent assumptions about global or shared variables. The defect lives in how the modules interact, so it is an interface/integration fault.

questiontext.text: Consider this dependency graph: Main calls A and B; A calls C; B calls C and D (so C is a shared utility called by both A and B; D is a leaf). Using bottom-up integration, which module should be integrated earliest?

answer.text: C — it is a leaf utility called by both A and B, so it must be available before A or B can be tested with real callees

feedback.text: Correct — bottom-up integrates leaves first, and the shared utility C is needed by both A and B.

answer.text: Main — because it is the top of the hierarchy

feedback.text: Integrating the root first is top-down; bottom-up starts with the leaves.

answer.text: A — because it appears before B alphabetically

feedback.text: A is not a leaf (it calls C); bottom-up integrates the leaf C before A.

answer.text: B — because it has the most callees

feedback.text: B is not a leaf (it calls C and D); its callees must be integrated first.

generalfeedback.text: Bottom-up integrates from the leaves up. C and D are the leaves; the shared utility C is called by both A and B, so it should be integrated first (with a driver) before A and B can be integrated against real callees.

questiontext.text: As each new module is added during incremental integration, the previously passing integration tests are re-run to check that the new module has not broken existing interactions. This activity is called:

answer.text: Regression testing

feedback.text: Correct — re-running earlier tests after a change guards against newly introduced breakage.

answer.text: Stub replacement

feedback.text: Replacing a stub is part of proceeding with integration, not the re-testing of prior interactions.

answer.text: Unit testing

feedback.text: Unit testing checks a single module in isolation, not the re-verification of prior integrated interactions.

answer.text: Acceptance testing

feedback.text: Acceptance testing validates the finished system against user needs, not the effect of each newly added module.

generalfeedback.text: Each newly integrated module can perturb interactions that already worked. Re-running the earlier integration tests to confirm nothing was broken is regression testing — an ongoing cost of incremental integration.

name.text: Top-down stubs with a shared utility

questiontext.text: Consider this dependency graph: Main calls A and B; A calls C; B calls C and D (C is shared, D is a leaf). Using top-down integration, the integrated set is exactly {Main, A, B}. How many stubs must be in place?

feedback.text: Correct — the absent callees are C (called by both A and B, but one stub) and D, giving 2 stubs.
C is called by both A and B, but it needs only one stub; with D that is 2 stubs, not 3.
Two distinct modules are absent (C and D), so one stub is too few.
Only C and D are absent; Main, A, and B are integrated, so 2 stubs suffice.

generalfeedback.text: With integrated set {Main, A, B}, the calls to absent modules are A→C, B→C, and B→D. C needs only a single stub even though two modules call it, so the distinct stubs are for C and D = 2 stubs.

name.text: Bottom-up scaffolding when the callee is already integrated

questiontext.text: Consider this call tree: P calls Q and R; Q calls S; R calls S (S is a shared leaf). Using bottom-up integration, S has already been integrated and you now integrate Q. How much scaffolding does integrating Q require?

answer.text: 1 driver and 0 stubs

feedback.text: Correct — Q's caller P is absent (so a driver is needed), but Q's callee S is already integrated (so no stub is needed).

answer.text: 1 driver and 1 stub

feedback.text: No stub is needed for S: S is already integrated, so Q can call the real S.

answer.text: 0 drivers and 1 stub

feedback.text: Bottom-up needs a driver here because Q's caller P is not integrated; and S is real, so no stub.

answer.text: 2 drivers and 0 stubs

feedback.text: Only Q is under test, so a single driver suffices.

generalfeedback.text: Integrating Q bottom-up: its callee S is already integrated, so Q calls the real S (0 stubs). Its caller P is absent, so one driver is written to invoke Q. Total: 1 driver, 0 stubs.

name.text: Stub can mask a low-level defect

questiontext.text: In top-down integration, a stub can mask a defect in the real lower-level module because the stub returns simplified, pre-arranged results instead of running the real logic.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — until the stub is replaced by the real module, the actual (possibly buggy) low-level behaviour is never exercised.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Stubs really can hide low-level defects: they return canned values rather than executing the real, possibly faulty, code.

generalfeedback.text: A stub is an oversimplified stand-in that returns fixed results. While it substitutes for a real module, that module's genuine logic — and any defect in it — is not run, so top-down integration can hide low-level defects until the stub is replaced.

name.text: Sandwich needs both stubs and drivers

questiontext.text: Sandwich (hybrid) integration requires both stubs and drivers.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — its top-down part uses stubs for lower modules while its bottom-up part uses drivers for the modules under test.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Sandwich combines top-down (stubs) and bottom-up (drivers), so it needs both kinds of scaffolding.

generalfeedback.text: Because sandwich integration works top-down on the upper layers (needing stubs for their callees) and bottom-up on the lower layers (needing drivers to call them), it requires both stubs and drivers at once.
